Mumbai: As dengue continues to claim lives and strain healthcare systems across India every monsoon, the country has taken a significant step towards strengthening its fight against the mosquito-borne disease. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has approved Qdenga, India's first dengue vaccine, marking a major milestone in the country's efforts to prevent one of its fastest-growing vector-borne diseases.The approval comes at a time when the reported burden of dengue in India has risen sharply. Reported dengue cases have increased 11-fold over the past two decades, according to the study Dengue in India: Temporal and Spatial Expansion in Last Two Decades by the Society of Medical Arthropodology (SOMA). In 2025, reported dengue cases exceeded 113,000, according to data from the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC). However, researchers believe the true burden is far higher, with modelling studies estimating that India records tens of millions of dengue infections each year.Developed by Japanese biopharmaceutical firm Takeda, the vaccine can be administered to individuals aged 4 to 60 years, including those who have previously been exposed to dengue. The vaccine is expected to reach the Indian market by early 2027 and is designed to induce a strong immune response by generating detectable antibodies against all four dengue virus serotypes—DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. ETHealthworld spoke to doctors to understand how this approval could reshape dengue prevention and why it represents a landmark moment in India's public-health journey. According to the study, moderate rainfall during the summer monsoon is associated with higher dengue mortality, while heavy rainfall can temporarily reduce transmission through a flushing effect. Warm temperatures above 27°C and humidity levels between 60 per cent and 78 per cent further elevate the risk of dengue. Dr. Prachi Sankhe, Consultant, Internal Medicine Physician, Apollo Hospitals Navi Mumbai, said, "Urbanisation, changing rainfall patterns and increasing population density have all contributed to the growing burden of dengue across many parts of India."She added, "For hospitals, the impact is most visible during seasonal surges, when large numbers of patients present with fever requiring evaluation and monitoring. Those who develop warning signs or severe dengue often require admission and intensive supportive care." Against this backdrop, Dr Vasant Nagvekar, Director, Infectious Diseases, Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, Mumbai, described the approval as a long-awaited development. "It's very painful to see people suffering from a mosquito-borne disease that is entirely preventable. India continues to bear one of the world's highest dengue burdens, with the disease now both epidemic and endemic. The availability of this vaccine is a major step forward because dengue continues to cause severe illness, hospitalisation and avoidable deaths," Dr Nagvekar added. Dr Nagvekar said, "I expect the vaccine to cut hospitalisations by nearly 80 per cent to 90 per cent. Even if people develop dengue after vaccination, the illness is expected to be much milder—similar to how influenza vaccines reduce disease severity. Fewer hospitalisations will naturally translate into lower mortality. If adopted widely through a mass immunisation programme, the vaccine could also contribute to herd immunity." Taking an intensivist lens, Dr Sanjith Saseedharan, Director, Critical Care, S. L. Raheja Hospital, Mahim, "I have seen dengue progress rapidly from what appears to be a mild fever to shock, bleeding and multi-organ failure. Even a meaningful reduction in severe dengue could save lives, ease pressure on hospital wards and intensive care units, and reduce the financial and emotional burden on families." However, doctors emphasised that vaccination alone will not eliminate dengue. Dr Saseedharan said, "The approval represents a shift in India's dengue strategy—from reacting to outbreaks to preventing infections and complications. However, vaccination must complement, not replace, mosquito control measures, early recognition of warning signs and timely medical care." The company is yet to announce pricing and commercial availability. Meanwhile doctors believe close collaboration between the government and the private sector will be essential to maximise the vaccine's impact. "Ideally, the vaccine should be rolled out through both the public and private sectors so that it becomes widely accessible to people across the country," Dr Nagvekar said. Against this backdrop, Dr Vasant Nagvekar, Director, Infectious Diseases, Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, Mumbai, described the approval as a long-awaited development. "It's very painful to see people suffering from a mosquito-borne disease that is entirely preventable. India continues to bear one of the world's highest dengue burdens, with the disease now both epidemic and endemic. The availability of this vaccine is a major step forward because dengue continues to cause severe illness, hospitalisation and avoidable deaths," Dr Nagvekar added. Dr Nagvekar said, "I expect the vaccine to cut hospitalisations by nearly 80 per cent to 90 per cent. Even if people develop dengue after vaccination, the illness is expected to be much milder—similar to how influenza vaccines reduce disease severity. Fewer hospitalisations will naturally translate into lower mortality. If adopted widely through a mass immunisation programme, the vaccine could also contribute to herd immunity." Taking an intensivist lens, Dr Sanjith Saseedharan, Director, Critical Care, S. L. Raheja Hospital, Mahim, "I have seen dengue progress rapidly from what appears to be a mild fever to shock, bleeding and multi-organ failure. Even a meaningful reduction in severe dengue could save lives, ease pressure on hospital wards and intensive care units, and reduce the financial and emotional burden on families." However, doctors emphasised that vaccination alone will not eliminate dengue. Dr Saseedharan said, "The approval represents a shift in India's dengue strategy—from reacting to outbreaks to preventing infections and complications. However, vaccination must complement, not replace, mosquito control measures, early recognition of warning signs and timely medical care." The company is yet to announce pricing and commercial availability. Meanwhile doctors believe close collaboration between the government and the private sector will be essential to maximise the vaccine's impact. "Ideally, the vaccine should be rolled out through both the public and private sectors so that it becomes widely accessible to people across the country," Dr Nagvekar said. In 2025, reported dengue cases exceeded 113,000, according to data from the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC). However, researchers believe the true burden is far higher, with modelling studies estimating that India records tens of millions of dengue infections each year.Developed by Japanese biopharmaceutical firm Takeda, the vaccine can be administered to individuals aged 4 to 60 years, including those who have previously been exposed to dengue. Warm temperatures above 27°C and humidity levels between 60 per cent and 78 per cent further elevate the risk of dengue. India continues to bear one of the world's highest dengue burdens, with the disease now both epidemic and endemic. The availability of this vaccine is a major step forward because dengue continues to cause severe illness, hospitalisation and avoidable deaths," Dr Nagvekar added. Reducing hospitalisations and severe disease Doctors believe the most immediate public-health impact of vaccination will be a reduction in severe disease, hospitalisations and, ultimately, dengue-related deaths.Dr Nagvekar said, "I expect the vaccine to cut hospitalisations by nearly 80 per cent to 90 per cent. Even if people develop dengue after vaccination, the illness is expected to be much milder—similar to how influenza vaccines reduce disease severity. Fewer hospitalisations will naturally translate into lower mortality. If adopted widely through a mass immunisation programme, the vaccine could also contribute to herd immunity." Taking an intensivist lens, Dr Sanjith Saseedharan, Director, Critical Care, S. L. Raheja Hospital, Mahim, "I have seen dengue progress rapidly from what appears to be a mild fever to shock, bleeding and multi-organ failure. Even a meaningful reduction in severe dengue could save lives, ease pressure on hospital wards and intensive care units, and reduce the financial and emotional burden on families." However, doctors emphasised that vaccination alone will not eliminate dengue. Dr Saseedharan said, "The approval represents a shift in India's dengue strategy—from reacting to outbreaks to preventing infections and complications. However, vaccination must complement, not replace, mosquito control measures, early recognition of warning signs and timely medical care." The road ahead Takeda said the vaccine is expected to become available through private healthcare facilities by early 2027. Asked about discussions with the government on wider deployment, Peter Streibl, General Manager, Southeast Asia and India Cluster, Takeda, told ETHealthworld, "Takeda's goal is to provide broad access to all eligible individuals through inclusion in National Immunisation Programmes (NIPs). However, wider availability through public health systems will depend on independent scientific and policy decisions taken by health authorities."The company is yet to announce pricing and commercial availability. Meanwhile doctors believe close collaboration between the government and the private sector will be essential to maximise the vaccine's impact. "Ideally, the vaccine should be rolled out through both the public and private sectors so that it becomes widely accessible to people across the country," Dr Nagvekar said. India World Sport Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health India’s dengue burden grows more complex as multiple virus strains circulate together, study finds The two-year nationwide surveillance study by the ICMR-VRDL network reveals increased risk of severe disease, and fresh challenges for the rollout of future dengue vaccination programmes Published - July 28, 2026 07:28 pm IST - NEW DELHIBindu Shajan PerappadanREAD LATER SEE ALL Remove There are four dengue serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) and severity depends more on secondary infection than serotype, although DENV-2 has often been linked to severe outbreaks. File image for representation only | Photo Credit: Sandeep Saxena India may be entering a more perilous phase in its dengue epidemic, with multiple strains of the virus now circulating simultaneously across much of the country, raising concerns over an increased risk of severe disease, and posing fresh challenges for the rollout of future dengue vaccination programmes.A two-year nationwide surveillance study by the Indian Council of Medical Research’s (ICMR) Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (VRDL) network found that all four dengue virus serotypes are circulating together in several parts of the country, with nearly one in 14 patients infected with more than one serotype at the same time. India’s first dengue vaccine arrives with a crucial safety caveatThe study, titled ‘Pan-India Molecular Surveillance of Dengue Serotypes, 2023–2025’, analysed 6,889 laboratory-confirmed dengue samples from 45 laboratories across 25 States and Union Territories and found that DENV-2 remained the predominant serotype, accounting for over half of all infections. However, researchers said the broader concern was the widespread co-circulation of multiple serotypes, indicating dengue hyper-endemicity.Eight States and Union Territories reported the presence of all four serotypes, while 15 reported three circulating simultaneously. Around 7% of patients were infected with two or more dengue serotypes concurrently. QDENGA: Can the new Japanese vaccine end the dengue menace in India? | In Focus PodcastThe study also found that patients with concurrent infections were more likely to develop severe manifestations of dengue, including dangerously low platelet counts, bleeding complications and severe joint pain, compared with those infected with a single serotype. While the findings need confirmation through long-term clinical studies, they suggest that simultaneous infection with multiple strains could worsen disease severity.There are four dengue serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) and severity depends more on secondary infection than serotype, although DENV-2 has often been linked to severe outbreaks. The emergence of hyperendemic transmission has implications beyond clinical care, the report notes. India currently has no dengue vaccine in its Universal Immunisation Programme, although indigenous vaccine candidates are in advanced stages of clinical development, and an internationally approved vaccine recently received regulatory clearance for import and sale in India. Researchers look at biomarkers which can predict dengue severityContinuous surveillance of circulating serotypes would be critical because vaccine effectiveness varies against different dengue strains, and shifts in the dominant serotype could influence both outbreak intensity and vaccine performance, researchers said.“Apart from routine steps taken to prevent mosquito breeding, there is certainly a need to incorporate the dengue vaccine into public health programmes, initially targeting endemic areas,” Gautam Menon, Professor of Physics and Biology, Ashoka University, said, speaking about the need for continuous surveillance. “But we also need more regular studies that can alert us about the magnitude of the problem, identify hotspots, and provide early warnings on how serotypes are shifting. This should be an ongoing, regularly reported study,” he added. While the findings need confirmation through long-term clinical studies, they suggest that simultaneous infection with multiple strains could worsen disease severity.There are four dengue serotypes (DENV-1 to 4) and severity depends more on secondary infection than serotype, although DENV-2 has often been linked to severe outbreaks. The emergence of hyperendemic transmission has implications beyond clinical care, the report notes. India currently has no dengue vaccine in its Universal Immunisation Programme, although indigenous vaccine candidates are in advanced stages of clinical development, and an internationally approved vaccine recently received regulatory clearance for import and sale in India. This should be an ongoing, regularly reported study,” he added. news.content: Dengue surge raises concerns as DENV-3 becomes dominant in Malaysia Local Health & Fitness 25 Jul 2026 • 8:22 AM MYT Twentytwo13 Twentytwo13 brings you insights on issues that matter to the people. PETALING JAYA: Dr Koh Kar Chai, Public Education and Advocacy Lead of Dengue Prevention Advocacy Malaysia (DPAM), says the emergence of DENV-3 as the dominant circulating dengue strain is a significant development, as most Malaysians have had limited exposure to it. As of July 23, the Health Ministry recorded 48,647dengue cases nationwide, a 49.9 per cent increase compared with the same period last year. Dengue-related deaths also rose sharply by 89,47 per cent, from 19 to 36. “DENV-3 is currently the dominant dengue strain in the country, unlike previous years when DENV-1 and DENV-2 were the more common circulating serotypes,” Dr Koh told Twentytwo13. “It is significant because most people have not been exposed to this strain before, which could lead to a sharp increase in dengue infections.” Although DENV-3 is not inherently more infectious than the other dengue serotypes, Dr Koh said the shift raises public health concerns because many Malaysians previously infected with DENV-1 or DENV-2 remain susceptible to DENV-3. “People who were previously infected with either DENV-1 or DENV-2 remain susceptible to DENV-3. If they contract a secondary infection, they are at greater risk of developing severe dengue due to what we call antibody-dependent enhancement,” he said. “Many people are unaware that there are four dengue serotypes, meaning a person can contract dengue up to four times in their lifetime. “There is a common misconception that a person who has had dengue once is immune for life. This belief must be dispelled, as a subsequent infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe dengue.” The Health Ministry attributed the rise in cases to several factors, including dengue’s cyclical transmission pattern, favourable weather conditions, rapid urbanisation, persistent mosquito breeding sites and the emergence of DENV-3 as the dominant circulating serotype. The Klang Valley continues to bear the greatest burden of infections, with Selangor recording more than 19,300 cases, followed by Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya with almost 8,000. Higher case numbers have also been reported in Johor, Sabah, Negeri Sembilan, Perak, Sarawak, Perlis, Terengganu and Labuan. Dr Koh said the emergence of DENV-3 does not fundamentally change existing dengue prevention strategies, but should serve as a timely reminder for Malaysians to strengthen preventive efforts. “The core messages of current dengue prevention campaigns remain the same, but the emergence of DENV-3 should serve as an impetus to intensify these campaigns and alert the public that we may face an increase in severe dengue cases,” he said. The Health Ministry likewise stressed that although the outbreak follows Malaysia’s familiar cyclical pattern, all stakeholders must remain vigilant. The ministry continues to strengthen surveillance, vector control, community engagement and predictive monitoring using climate and geospatial data to identify high-risk areas. Children remain among the groups most vulnerable to severe dengue, particularly if they have previously been infected with a different serotype. “Children are definitely at greater risk of severe dengue if infected with DENV-3, especially if they have had a previous dengue infection,” Dr Koh said. “But this risk is not directly related to DENV-3 itself. Rather, it is because they have previously been infected with a different dengue strain. “Parents are advised to seek medical attention promptly if their child develops a high fever to ensure a proper diagnosis and avoid possible dengue-related complications.” He urged the public to watch for warning signs of severe dengue, including persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, extreme lethargy, rapid breathing and restlessness, all of which require immediate medical attention. Despite the sharp increase in cases and deaths, Dr Koh said the focus should remain on prevention rather than fear. “There are various factors driving the increase in both infections and mortality,” he said. “The public should recognise that dengue is an endemic disease that can be fatal, and actively adopt the preventive measures promoted through various dengue awareness campaigns, including vaccination.” The Health Ministry has urged Malaysians to conduct weekly inspections to eliminate stagnant water, participate in community clean-up activities and seek prompt medical treatment if dengue symptoms develop. The ministry stressed that sustained public participation remains one of the country’s strongest defences against the disease. View Original Article 209 20 What Do Netizens Say? As of July 23, 48,647 cases have been recorded nationwide, a 49.9% increase from last year, with deaths rising sharply to 36. The Klang Valley is most affected, with Selangor reporting over 19,300 cases. Authorities are intensifying surveillance and prevention efforts, urging the public to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek prompt medical attention for symptoms.

news.content_title: The Potential for Antivirals in Dengue Prophylaxis and Treatment
news.content: A study found that the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir reduced dengue virus infection RNA levels and symptoms in a controlled setting, supporting its potential as a prophylactic option. Dengue virus infection, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV- 1-4), has an expanding global incidence and geographic range 1 with locally acquired cases to Europe and the United States. 2 While its cases are often mild or asymptomatic, dengue has the potential to cause severe illness, including shock and capillary leak syndrome, in both dengue-naive individuals and those with prior infection. Two vaccines have received worldwide approval for the prevention and long-term protection against reinfection. CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia; Sanofi) is approved for use in certain endemic areas among those aged 9 to 45 years with confirmed prior dengue infection. However, it is not approved for travelers and is being discontinued due to low demand. TAK-003 (Qdenga; Takeda) is approved in many countries for both seropositive and seronegative people. Despite vaccine development and availability, there are no approved antiviral prophylaxis or treatments against dengue, especially in those who are nonimmune. Mosnodenvir is an orally administered small-molecule agent developed to target dengue viral replication. The drug inhibits the de novo formation of the NS4B-NS3 complex. NS4B is a transmembrane protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, which binds NS3 to enhance NS3 helicase activity and increase viral replication. 3 Preclinical studies have shown serotype-independent antiviral activity through in vitro and in vivo models, and recent phase 1 trials have demonstrated an acceptable safety profile. 4 This FIGURE represents the viral replication complex of Dengue virus and the target of mosnodenvir. The NS4B complex is ER (endoplasmic reticulum) bound. 5 Durbin and colleagues conducted a phase 2a trial that assessed the antiviral activity and safety of mosnodenvir in healthy participants who received a challenge virus with a hypoattenuated strain of DENV-3. 6 This was designed as a doubleblind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Vermont, with funding from Johnson & Johnson. Healthy adults aged 18 to 55 years with no prior dengue exposure or endemic travel were enrolled and assigned to mosnodenvir or placebo in a stepwise, dose-escalation design. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 200-mg loading dose of oral mosnodenvir or placebo for the 5 days prior to challenge, and received an inoculation of underattenuated DENV-3 on day 0. The participants were then enrolled 2:1 into a high-dose cohort to establish safety. Further participants were randomly assigned to a high (100 mg), medium (50 mg), or low (10 mg) dose vs placebo in a 3:3:1 ratio for maintenance from day 1 to day 21. Patients were then followed through day 85. Primary outcomes included a reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels, clinical symptoms of infection, serologic response, and safety. The trial was powered to 85% probability to detect a 30% difference in RNA load between groups. High-dose mosnodenvir was associated with a significant reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels compared with placebo, with a clear dose-dependent antiviral effect regarding reduction in RNA levels and dengue infection–related symptoms. Participants with undetectable viral RNA did not have any detectable neutralizing antibodies, suggesting that successful inhibition of viral replication may prevent the development of humoral immunity. Mosnodenvir was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events. Only 2 severe events were noted: infection with SARS-CoV-2, and severe elevation in lipase and glucose levels. Together, the findings support mosnodenvir as a promising antiviral for dengue prophylaxis against DENV-3 infection, especially at high doses. However, the small sample size, use of a hypoattenuated DENV-3 challenge strain, and controlled timing of exposure limit generalizability to real-world settings with unpredictable exposure and multiple circulating serotypes. There is further work to be done to study those who have already been infected, those living in endemic regions, and the timing of prophylaxis. Despite these encouraging early results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. 7 However, other dengue antiviral strategies remain in development, including agents that target antiviral replication by Novartis, which are undergoing a phase 2 trial. 8 There is also a monoclonal antibody undergoing evaluation. 9 These show promise for the future of prophylaxis and treatment for dengue virus in the seropositive and seronegative populations. selected_identity.page_title: The Potential for Antivirals in Dengue Prophylaxis and Treatment

news.content_original: A study found that the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir reduced dengue virus infection RNA levels and symptoms in a controlled setting, supporting its potential as a prophylactic option. Dengue virus infection, transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and caused by 4 distinct serotypes (DENV- 1-4), has an expanding global incidence and geographic range 1 with locally acquired cases to Europe and the United States. 2 While its cases are often mild or asymptomatic, dengue has the potential to cause severe illness, including shock and capillary leak syndrome, in both dengue-naive individuals and those with prior infection. Two vaccines have received worldwide approval for the prevention and long-term protection against reinfection. CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia; Sanofi) is approved for use in certain endemic areas among those aged 9 to 45 years with confirmed prior dengue infection. However, it is not approved for travelers and is being discontinued due to low demand. TAK-003 (Qdenga; Takeda) is approved in many countries for both seropositive and seronegative people. Despite vaccine development and availability, there are no approved antiviral prophylaxis or treatments against dengue, especially in those who are nonimmune. Mosnodenvir is an orally administered small-molecule agent developed to target dengue viral replication. The drug inhibits the de novo formation of the NS4B-NS3 complex. NS4B is a transmembrane protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, which binds NS3 to enhance NS3 helicase activity and increase viral replication. 3 Preclinical studies have shown serotype-independent antiviral activity through in vitro and in vivo models, and recent phase 1 trials have demonstrated an acceptable safety profile. 4 This FIGURE represents the viral replication complex of Dengue virus and the target of mosnodenvir. The NS4B complex is ER (endoplasmic reticulum) bound. 5 Durbin and colleagues conducted a phase 2a trial that assessed the antiviral activity and safety of mosnodenvir in healthy participants who received a challenge virus with a hypoattenuated strain of DENV-3. 6 This was designed as a doubleblind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Vermont, with funding from Johnson & Johnson. Healthy adults aged 18 to 55 years with no prior dengue exposure or endemic travel were enrolled and assigned to mosnodenvir or placebo in a stepwise, dose-escalation design. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive a 200-mg loading dose of oral mosnodenvir or placebo for the 5 days prior to challenge, and received an inoculation of underattenuated DENV-3 on day 0. The participants were then enrolled 2:1 into a high-dose cohort to establish safety. Further participants were randomly assigned to a high (100 mg), medium (50 mg), or low (10 mg) dose vs placebo in a 3:3:1 ratio for maintenance from day 1 to day 21. Patients were then followed through day 85. Primary outcomes included a reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels, clinical symptoms of infection, serologic response, and safety. The trial was powered to 85% probability to detect a 30% difference in RNA load between groups. High-dose mosnodenvir was associated with a significant reduction in DENV-3 RNA levels compared with placebo, with a clear dose-dependent antiviral effect regarding reduction in RNA levels and dengue infection–related symptoms. Participants with undetectable viral RNA did not have any detectable neutralizing antibodies, suggesting that successful inhibition of viral replication may prevent the development of humoral immunity. Mosnodenvir was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events. Only 2 severe events were noted: infection with SARS-CoV-2, and severe elevation in lipase and glucose levels. Together, the findings support mosnodenvir as a promising antiviral for dengue prophylaxis against DENV-3 infection, especially at high doses. However, the small sample size, use of a hypoattenuated DENV-3 challenge strain, and controlled timing of exposure limit generalizability to real-world settings with unpredictable exposure and multiple circulating serotypes. There is further work to be done to study those who have already been infected, those living in endemic regions, and the timing of prophylaxis. Despite these encouraging early results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. 7 However, other dengue antiviral strategies remain in development, including agents that target antiviral replication by Novartis, which are undergoing a phase 2 trial. 8 There is also a monoclonal antibody undergoing evaluation. 9 These show promise for the future of prophylaxis and treatment for dengue virus in the seropositive and seronegative populations. analysis.brief_en: A recent phase 2a trial evaluated the investigational antiviral mosnodenvir for dengue prophylaxis in healthy adults without prior dengue exposure. Conducted at Johns Hopkins University and the University of Vermont, the double-blind, placebo-controlled study found that high-dose mosnodenvir significantly reduced DENV-3 RNA levels and infection-related symptoms. The drug showed a dose-dependent antiviral effect and was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate adverse events. Despite these promising results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. However, other antiviral strategies, including agents from Novartis and a monoclonal antibody, are still in progress, offering hope for future dengue prevention and treatment options.

Despite these promising results, Johnson & Johnson has discontinued further development of mosnodenvir. However, other antiviral strategies, including agents from Novartis and a monoclonal antibody, are still in progress, offering hope for future dengue prevention and treatment options.

elements_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在约翰霍普金斯大学和佛蒙特大学进行的。参与者是 18 至 55 岁的健康成年人,之前没有接触过登革热,也没有登革热流行史。
elements_zh.event: 一项 2a 期试验在接受 DENV-3 低减毒株攻击的健康参与者中评估了 mosnodenvir(一种研究性 抗病毒药物)的 抗病毒药物 活性和安全性。该试验是一项由强生公司资助的双盲、随机、安慰剂对照研究。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 与安慰剂相比,高剂量莫诺登韦与 DENV-3 RNA 水平显着降低相关,显示出剂量依赖性 抗病毒药物 效应。该药物总体耐受性良好,不良事件大多为轻度至中度。然而,小样本量和低减毒 DENV-3 挑战菌株的使用限制了对现实世界环境的普遍适用性。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该试验证明了 mosnodenvir 作为 DENV-3 预防选择的可接受的安全性和有前景的 抗病毒药物 活性。然而,强生公司已停止进一步开发莫诺登韦。其他登革热 抗病毒药物 策略,包括诺华的药物和单克隆抗体,仍在开发中。

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该研究是在约翰霍普金斯大学和佛蒙特大学进行的。参与者是 18 至 55 岁的健康成年人,之前没有接触过登革热,也没有登革热流行史。
analysis_zh.event: 一项 2a 期试验在接受 DENV-3 低减毒株攻击的健康参与者中评估了 mosnodenvir(一种研究性 抗病毒药物)的 抗病毒药物 活性和安全性。该试验是一项由强生公司资助的双盲、随机、安慰剂对照研究。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 与安慰剂相比,高剂量莫诺登韦与 DENV-3 RNA 水平显着降低相关,显示出剂量依赖性 抗病毒药物 效应。该药物总体耐受性良好,不良事件大多为轻度至中度。然而,小样本量和低减毒 DENV-3 挑战菌株的使用限制了对现实世界环境的普遍适用性。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该试验证明了 mosnodenvir 作为 DENV-3 预防选择的可接受的安全性和有前景的 抗病毒药物 活性。然而,强生公司已停止进一步开发莫诺登韦。其他登革热 抗病毒药物 策略,包括诺华的药物和单克隆抗体,仍在开发中。

news.content: Philstar Home The Philippine Star Pilipino Star Ngayon The Freeman CEBU NEWS OPINION METRO CEBU REGION CEBU BUSINESS CEBU SPORTS CEBU LIFESTYLE CEBU ENTERTAINMENT SUPPORT PHILSTAR Pang-Masa Banat Close the sidebar No outbreak yet: Capitol on guard against dengue By Jonnavie Villa(The Freeman) - July 30, 2026 - 12:00am Facebook Twitter CEBU, Philippines — Despite recording 381 confirmed dengue cases across Cebu Province in July, provincial health officials clarified that the situation has not reached outbreak level, although the steady rise in infections has prompted intensified surveillance and heightened hospital preparedness. Capitol Public Health Consultant Dr. Nikki Catalan described the increase as typical during the rainy season but emphasized that the province remains in a "guarded" situation rather than an epidemiological outbreak. Provincial Health Office (PHO) data showed Toledo City recorded the highest number of confirmed dengue cases with 49, followed by Barili with 39, Talisay City with 34, Consolacion with 33, and Carcar City and Medellin with 19 cases each. Cordova and Dalaguete each reported 17 cases, followed by Sogod with 14, Danao City with 13, and Argao, Balamban and Compostela with 12 cases each. Liloan logged 10 cases, while Daanbantayan, Moalboal and San Francisco recorded nine infections each. Borbon, Minglanilla and Oslob registered eight cases each, followed by Badian, Bogo City and Madridejos with seven each, Pinamungajan with five, and Catmon with four. Rainy season spike Dr. Jenina Canoy, PHO chief of hospitals, said the increase in dengue cases coincides with the onset of the rainy season, when mosquito breeding sites become more prevalent. "Ni-spike jud siya nu considering that we're in the rainy season," said Canoy. She said the PHO had already reminded local government units before the rainy season to strengthen dengue prevention measures during coordination meetings. Canoy added that Capitol-run hospitals had prepared in advance by ensuring adequate stocks of medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and sufficient personnel to respond to the anticipated increase in dengue patients. To improve patient management, the provincial government has activated Dengue Fast Lanes in all Capitol-run provincial and district hospitals. Canoy said the initiative enables hospitals to immediately prioritize patients with suspected dengue upon arrival. "Among gi-prepare ang hospitals jud nga ma-kompleto ang supplies necessary, to have this priority lanes for dengue patients so that they can be attended timely," she said. She stressed that activating the fast lanes is part of the province's preparedness strategy and not a response to an outbreak. "In this time amo lang jud gi-activate just to be more prepared with regards to our medicine, supplies, IV fluids, preparation of the staff so that they will be able to cater to patients immediately," Canoy added. Under the system, patients exhibiting signs and symptoms of dengue undergo priority assessment, faster laboratory testing and immediate medical management, allowing health workers to closely monitor cases that could progress into severe dengue. On guard Catalan said dengue cases have continued to rise over the past three months, prompting health authorities to intensify surveillance across the province. "In the past three months ni-saka na jud ang cases," said Catalan. Despite the increase, she emphasized that the number of cases remains below the threshold needed to declare an outbreak. "We'd say guarded. Dili pa matawag nga outbreak but just of concern because of the rise of the cases. Epidemiologically, dili siya outbreak," she said. Instead, Catalan said the province has adopted a more aggressive approach to detecting and treating suspected cases through the Dengue Fast Lanes. "But right now we're more vigilant. Mao ni ang Dengue Fast Lanes. Point being there's a higher or lower tolerance for these kinds of signs and symptoms—deretso na sila didto," she added. Early detection Catalan urged residents not to panic over the increase in cases but to seek medical attention immediately once symptoms develop. "We're really not here to cause panic or fear, but mao lang jud ni ang among gibalik-balik—early detection, early treatment saves lives," she said. She stressed that prompt consultation significantly improves a patient's chances of avoiding severe complications. "The earlier to seek care the better jud. Mao lang na among gi-advocate," Catalan said. Health officials continue to closely monitor dengue alongside leptospirosis, another disease that commonly surges during the rainy season. Earlier PHO monitoring recorded two dengue-related deaths during the current surveillance period—one each from Consolacion and Compostela. Children aged six to 10 years old account for the highest number of infections, followed by individuals aged 11 to 20 years old. Catalan also urged local government units to sustain regular clean-up drives and closely monitor dengue trends within their respective communities to help curb transmission. Blood supply concerns Apart from monitoring cases, Catalan raised concerns over the limited supply of blood products needed by some dengue patients requiring transfusions. She said blood remains available through blood banks but acknowledged that supplies of specific blood components can become scarce. "Nihit jud... In my personal experience because I have a family friend nga nangita jud og dugo," Catalan shared. Canoy said Capitol-run hospitals have scheduled regular mobile blood donation drives every two to three months, depending on each hospital's schedule. She added that the Philippine Red Cross continues to conduct blood donation activities in various cities, municipalities and schools to help maintain adequate blood supplies. Catalan said another bloodletting activity is scheduled on August 4 and 5 as part of the province's wellness caravan to encourage more voluntary blood donors. — /FPL (FREEMAN) SPONSORED ARTICLES SM Cinema Theater formats explained: Your guide to choosing the cinema that best suits you On the Radar July 29, 2026 - 5:25pm GCash brings 'Wais Tindera Caravan' to Cebu, empowering MSMEs with financial tools and responsible borrowing On the Radar July 28, 2026 - 5:00pm GCash brings 'Wais Tindera Caravan' to Cebu, empowering MSMEs with financial tools and responsible borrowing Technology July 28, 2026 - 5:00pm SM Cinema brings FIFA World Cup Final 2026 to the big screen On the Radar July 28, 2026 - 4:38pm Before your first overseas paycheck: 7 financial moves every Filipino professional should make The Budgetarian July 28, 2026 - 4:30pm Elevate everyday living with Acacia Supasleek collection by American Standard Modern Living July 28, 2026 - 3:00pm GCash gathers top global tech leaders shaping the future of AI and cybersecurity at the 5th iGnite Innovation Summit On the Radar July 28, 2026 - 2:02pm 'The Power of X' comes alive at PGDX 2026 On the Radar July 28, 2026 - 2:00pm Bonchon introduces Golden Crunch flavor to complete '7 Ways to Chikin' lineup Food and Leisure July 28, 2026 - 1:55pm Show comments Ad

elements_zh.location_and_population: 菲律宾宿务省,包括托莱多市、巴里利、塔里萨伊市、康索拉西翁、卡尔卡市、麦德林、科尔多瓦、达拉盖地、索戈德、达瑙市、阿尔高、巴兰班、孔波斯特拉、利洛安、达安班塔延、莫阿尔博阿尔、旧金山、博尔邦、明拉尼拉、奥斯洛布、巴迪安、博戈市、马德里德霍斯、皮纳蒙加詹等城市和直辖市卡特蒙。受影响人群中,6-10岁儿童是感染率最高的群体,其次是11-20岁人群。
elements_zh.event: 省卫生官员报告称,2026 年 7 月,宿务省确诊了 381 例登革热病例,并澄清说,情况尚未达到 暴发 水平,但由于感染人数稳步上升,正在密切监测。这种增加被描述为雨季期间的典型现象,该省仍处于“戒备”状态,而不是流行病学上的“暴发”。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 2026 年 7 月报告了 381 例确诊登革热病例,其中托莱多市病例数最多(49 例),其次是巴里利(39 例)、塔利萨伊市(34 例)、康索拉西翁(33 例)、卡尔卡市和麦德林(各 19 例)。记录了两例与登革热相关的死亡(康索拉西翁和孔波斯特拉各一例)。该省已在所有国会大厦运营的医院启动登革热快速通道,优先处理疑似病例。卫生官员对输血用血液供应有限表示担忧,但指出仍然可以通过血库获得血液。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 省卫生部门加强了监测并加强了医院的准备工作。国会大厦运营的医院已确保药品、静脉输液、医疗用品和人员的充足库存。登革热快车道已启动,优先评估、检测和管理疑似病例。提醒当地政府部门加强预防措施,定期开展清理工作。计划献血活动是为了解决供应问题。

news.content: In September 2024, a handful of patients showed up at the emergency room in the coastal city of Fano, Italy, with mysterious symptoms: a rash on their hands and feet, fever, nausea, and diarrhea. Doctors sent for various tests until one came back with a positive result for dengue, a viral infection spread by mosquitoes, usually in tropical regions of the world. They tested the other patients, and, sure enough, they had dengue too. The strange thing? None of the patients had recently traveled to a country where they might expect to pick up a dengue infection. The only thing they had in common was visiting a particular neighbourhood in Fano. As climate change increases temperatures across Europe, invasive mosquitoes are spreading and introducing disease agents that Europeans would usually think about only when traveling to other continents. The Fano outbreak wasn’t the first time dengue had been detected as spreading locally in mainland Europe, but it was significantly larger than previous incidents, with 199 cases detected between mid-August and mid-October of 2024. Over the past few years, European countries have reported outbreaks of other mosquito-borne viruses such as chikungunya, a painful disease that causes joint swelling, and West Nile virus. In a heating world, so-called tropical diseases are no longer restricted to tropical regions—and researchers expect the trend to continue. The main current culprit is the mosquito Aedes albopictus, commonly known as the Asian tiger mosquito (or just the tiger mosquito, given it’s now found across all continents). Unlike many mosquito species, it bites in the daytime as well as at night. The tiger mosquito already has established populations across Europe, particularly in the south, and we can expect it to move north, says Riccardo Moretti, a senior researcher at the Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA), who has been working on tiger mosquitos for more than 20 years. The tiger mosquito thrives between 20 and 30 degrees Celsius (68 to 86 Fahrenheit), but it can still live at around 10 Celsius (50 Fahrenheit). “This means that at the moment there are already conditions that could allow for the spread of the Asian tiger mosquito, even in England,” Moretti says. At the moment, these conditions are limited to the warmest part of the year in northern European countries. But farther south, such as in Greece, the mosquito season is elongating. Moretti says researchers have found adults buzzing around until December and reappearing already in March; they overwinter as eggs. “There is a concrete risk that in the next few years, we could have a population capable of surviving throughout the year,” Moretti says. At the moment, cases of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe tend to occur toward the end of summer. This is when tiger mosquitoes are most prevalent, and it’s also when more people return from travel. Someone unwittingly brings back an infection that isn’t found in Europe—dengue, say—and gets bitten by a tiger mosquito. The mosquito goes on to bite other people, and the disease spreads locally. But as the weather cools, the mosquitoes get less active and cases subside. If the mosquito season lasts longer, however, more infections can occur. Ultimately, says Moretti, there’s a risk that tropical diseases like dengue could become endemic in parts of Europe, meaning the disease is always there. “It is completely different dealing with occasional cases of virus transmission, and instead dealing with a permanent status of possibility of transmission,” he says. A difference of a couple of degrees can make a big difference. Earlier this year, a study found that the conditions required for tiger mosquitoes to transmit chikungunya were cooler than previously thought. The mosquitoes can spread the virus at just 14 degrees Celsius (57 degrees Fahrenheit) rather than 16 (61 degrees Fahrenheit), meaning outbreaks could occur in most European countries and for longer periods. “That difference of two degrees matters a lot when we are talking about global warming,” says Sandeep Tegar, an epidemiological modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, who led the study. While warmer temperatures may generally create better conditions for mosquitoes, this isn’t the full story. Too hot—more than 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit)—and tiger mosquitoes struggle to survive. Southern France and Spain, impacted by recent heat waves and wildfires, may actually have fewer mosquitoes this year, says Frederic Bartumeus, an ecologist at the Spanish scientific research center CEAB: “It’s not been a great mosquito season in these areas, because it’s too hot and it’s too dry.” Rain is important, as mosquitoes need standing water to breed: This is where they lay their eggs, and where the larvae and pupae develop. “If it rains too little, then there’s not sufficient breeding sites,” explains Felipe Colón González, technology lead and expert in climate and infectious diseases at the UK-based health foundation Wellcome. “But if it rains too much, then it can wash away the mosquito breeding sites.” Humidity also plays a role. Beyond mosquitoes, climate conditions can have different effects on the viruses they carry, and on the behavior of humans—an important consideration in the spread of disease. This all makes modeling patterns of mosquitoes and the diseases they spread more complex, so ongoing surveillance is critical. It may be possible to reduce mosquito populations if they’re caught early enough. ENEA’s Moretti is part of a team that recently ran an experiment to control a tiger mosquito population in Italy by releasing more than a million male mosquitoes that were reproductively incompatible—meaning when they mate, the female lays sterile eggs. This significantly reduced the number of fertile mosquito eggs in the area. But breeding mosquitoes in a specialized biofactory was expensive. In this case, the mosquitoes were bred in Miami by Google’s Debug program and shipped to Italy. In any case, it would be impossible to eliminate mosquitoes, Moretti says—they’re too efficient at colonizing new areas. “But what is important is to drastically reduce the risks of transmissions of tropical viruses.” Colón González says the main test for European countries is whether public health systems can keep isolated outbreaks from becoming major crises. “A common misconception is that preparedness is mainly about predicting disease outbreaks,” he says. “In reality, preparedness is about building the system that allows the public health infrastructure to effectively react when the risks emerge.” In this regard, Europe has an advantage over some parts of the world: Reliable public health and information systems mean that, so far, cases of mosquito-transmitted diseases have remained lower than in other areas of the world with a similar climate. As invasive mosquitoes continue to settle across the Continent, Europeans may have to get used to taking the kinds of precautions that people in tropical regions are accustomed to. In Spain, Bartumeus already has mosquito nets on his windows and regularly empties standing water, such as that left sitting in flower pots. He uses mosquito repellant and wears long trousers if he’s going to be outside in the evening. “Simple things like that, that’s the only thing you can do,” he says. Soon, the tiger mosquito may have company. Another invasive species, Aedes aegypti, or the yellow fever mosquito, has already established populations in Cyprus and the Portuguese archipelago of Madeira. As its name would suggest, it can transmit yellow fever, but it also carries dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. Yellow fever mosquitoes can’t tolerate temperatures quite as cool as the tiger mosquito can, but it has been detected making occasional jaunts north, likely transported on cargo. Its most recent destination: a service station in Luxembourg

news.title_zh: 登革热 和基孔肯雅热等热带疾病在欧洲呈上升趋势 - 连线
news.source_body_en: In September 2024, Italy experienced its largest local dengue outbreak in mainland Europe, with 199 cases reported in the coastal city of Fano between mid-August and mid-October. Notably, none of the patients had recently traveled to endemic regions, confirming local transmission. The outbreak highlights the growing threat of tropical diseases in Europe, driven by climate change and the spread of invasive mosquitoes like Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito). These mosquitoes, which thrive in warmer temperatures, have established populations across Europe and are expected to expand northward. Experts warn that even a slight increase in temperatures could enable year-round mosquito activity and endemic transmission of diseases like dengue, chikungunya, and West Nile virus. While public health systems in Europe have so far contained outbreaks, ongoing surveillance and adaptive measures are critical to mitigate future risks.
news.content_zh: 2024年9月,意大利经历了欧洲大陆最大规模的本地登革热暴发,8月中旬至10月中旬,沿海城市法诺报告了199例病例。值得注意的是,这些患者最近都没有去过流行地区,证实了当地的 传播。暴发 强调了在气候变化和白纹伊蚊(亚洲虎蚊)等入侵性蚊子传播的推动下,欧洲热带疾病的威胁日益严重。这些蚊子在温暖的气温下繁衍生息,已在欧洲各地建立种群,预计将向北扩张。专家警告说,即使气温略有升高,也可能导致蚊子全年活动,导致登革热、基孔肯雅热和西尼罗河病毒等地方性疾病流行。虽然欧洲的公共卫生系统迄今为止已经遏制了 监测,但持续进行的 监测 和适应性措施对于减轻未来风险至关重要。

Why Does Diabetes Make Dengue More Dangerous? Written by Dr. Nikitha Narayanan Medically Reviewed by Dr. Shanmathi Rajendran BDS on Jul 24 2026 2:43 PM Listen to this article 0:00/0:00 People with type 2 diabetes may face a higher risk of severe dengue complications, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome. Learn how diabetes influences dengue severity and why experts recommend integrating infectious disease prevention into diabetes care. Highlights: A review suggests people with type 2 diabetes are more likely to develop severe dengue complications High blood sugar may impair immunity and increase the risk of excessive inflammation during dengue infection Experts recommend considering dengue vaccination for eligible people with diabetes in dengue-endemic regions Dengue fever affects millions of people every year, but not everyone develops severe disease (1✔ ✔Trusted SourceDiabetes as risk factor to severity of dengue in naive patientsGo to source). According to a new review by diabetes and infectious disease experts, people living with type 2 diabetes are more likely to experience serious complications, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. The authors suggest that diabetes should be recognized as an important risk factor when planning dengue prevention strategies. Blood Sugar ChartThe blood sugar chart gives you the fasting glucose values and glucose tolerance test values for normal people and people with early diabetes and established diabetes. Also use the calculator to find out if you have diabetes. How Can High Blood Sugar Worsen Dengue Infection? Researchers explain that persistently elevated blood sugar can affect several parts of the immune system. Poorly controlled diabetes may: Reduce the body's ability to fight infections Damage blood vessels Promote chronic inflammation Increase the likelihood of an exaggerated immune response, sometimes called a cytokine storm During dengue infection, this excessive inflammatory response may contribute to: Dengue hemorrhagic fever Internal bleeding Plasma leakage Dengue shock syndrome Diabetes Risk Assessment CalculatorAlmost one-third of the people are unaware of the risk factors of diabetes. Find out if you run the risk of diabetes by using Diabetes Risk Assessment calculator.Why Diabetes May Increase Severe Dengue Risk Diabetes-Related Change Possible Effect During Dengue High blood sugar Impaired immune response. Blood vessel damage Greater risk of vascular leakage. Chronic inflammation Stronger inflammatory response. Cytokine storm Increased risk of severe dengue complications. Dengue Vaccine – Administer Only in High Burden RegionsNewly developed dengue vaccine should be used only if you are previously infected by the dengue virus. A blood test before taking the vaccine is recommended.Should Dengue Vaccination Become Part of Diabetes Care? One of the most important recommendations from the review is to consider integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes management, particularly in regions where dengue is common. The authors argue that preventing infection in high-risk individuals could reduce: Severe illness Hospitalization Complications Healthcare burden during outbreaks However, they do not recommend universal vaccination for everyone with diabetes. Vaccination policies should continue to follow national guidelines, vaccine eligibility criteria, and individual clinical assessment. DengiAll: Why India's First Dengue Vaccine is Being Watched WorldwideDengiAll emerges as a promising single-dose solution offering balanced protection against all four dengue types.Why Managing Chronic Diseases and Infectious Diseases Together Makes Sense Traditionally, diabetes care has focused on controlling blood sugar and preventing complications such as heart disease, kidney disease, and nerve damage. The review proposes a broader approach by integrating infectious disease prevention into routine diabetes care. This could include: Vaccination where appropriate Patient education during dengue season Early recognition of warning signs Prompt medical evaluation during fever Such an approach may improve outcomes in countries where dengue is endemic. Which Symptoms Need Immediate Medical Attention? People with diabetes who develop dengue should seek urgent medical care if they experience: Persistent vomiting Severe abdominal pain Bleeding from the gums or nose Blood in vomit or stools Extreme weakness Difficulty breathing Dizziness or fainting Reduced urine output These may indicate progression to severe dengue. What This Means for You People living with type 2 diabetes already face a higher risk of several long-term health complications. This review suggests they may also be more vulnerable to severe dengue, reinforcing the importance of preventing mosquito bites, maintaining good blood sugar control, and seeking early medical care if fever develops during dengue season. The authors also propose that dengue vaccination should be considered as part of comprehensive diabetes care in endemic regions. However, because this is a review paper rather than a new clinical trial, and because dengue vaccines have specific eligibility criteria, further research and public health guidance will be needed before such an approach becomes routine. Frequently Asked QuestionsQ: Does diabetes increase the risk of severe dengue?A: Evidence summarized in this review suggests that people with type 2 diabetes are more likely to develop severe dengue complications than those without diabetes.Q: Why does diabetes make dengue more severe?A: High blood sugar can impair immune function, damage blood vessels, and promote excessive inflammation, which may contribute to severe dengue.Q: Should everyone with diabetes get a dengue vaccine?A: Not necessarily. Dengue vaccination should follow national guidelines and individual eligibility criteria because current vaccines are not recommended for everyone.Q: Can good blood sugar control reduce dengue complications?A: Although this review did not directly study blood sugar control, maintaining good glucose control supports overall immune health and is generally recommended during infections.Q: What should people with diabetes do during dengue season?A: Prevent mosquito bites, control blood sugar, stay hydrated, and seek prompt medical attention if fever or dengue warning signs develop. analysis.brief_en: A recent review by diabetes and infectious disease experts highlights that individuals with type 2 diabetes may face a higher risk of severe dengue complications, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome. The review suggests that persistently elevated blood sugar can impair immune function, damage blood vessels, and promote excessive inflammation, potentially leading to more severe outcomes during dengue infection. Based on these findings, the authors recommend considering dengue vaccination as part of comprehensive diabetes care in regions where dengue is endemic. However, they emphasize that vaccination policies should follow national guidelines and individual eligibility criteria. The review also underscores the importance of mosquito bite prevention, maintaining good blood sugar control, and seeking early medical care if fever develops during dengue season for people with diabetes.

news.content_title: Dengue Fever Has Now Surpassed 500 U.S. Cases and the Mosquito That Spreads It Is Expanding North
news.content: Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One app. Start reading Get all your news in one place. 100's of premium titles. One news app. Start reading Medical Daily Cole Mercer Jul 24, 2026, 12:00 PM Dengue Fever Has Now Surpassed 500 U.S. Cases and the Mosquito That Spreads It Is Expanding North Florida CDC Los Angeles United States MMWR Public Health Dengue fever has surpassed 500 cases in the United States in 2026, following a record-breaking 2024 that saw 3,798 confirmed cases reported to the CDC's ArboNET surveillance system , a 359 percent increase above the 2010 to 2023 annual average. The mosquito primarily responsible for spreading the virus, Aedes aegypti, is now confirmed to be expanding its range northward into states well beyond its traditional subtropical stronghold. And this summer, the window for local transmission risk extends further into the continental United States than it did a decade ago. Public health authorities, entomologists, and infectious disease specialists are tracking the shift with concern. Dengue is not simply a travel disease any longer for Americans. While the vast majority of cases remain travel-associated, the conditions enabling local transmission are broadening with each passing season. Why This Matters Most people who contract dengue experience a flu-like illness and recover fully. But dengue is unusual among mosquito-borne diseases in that a second infection with a different dengue serotype, there are four, can trigger severe hemorrhagic fever. This condition causes the blood vessels to leak, platelets to drop, and in serious cases can lead to organ failure and death. There is currently no approved dengue vaccine recommended for general use in the continental United States, and no specific antiviral treatment. The cases most visible to U.S. readers are concentrated in Florida, where Miami-Dade County has maintained an active mosquito-borne illness alert through 2026. But the more significant public health story is what is happening further north. A peer-reviewed paper in the CDC's Emerging Infectious Diseases journal documented a seven-week chain of locally acquired dengue transmission in Los Angeles County in 2025, the kind of sustained community spread once considered impossible outside the subtropical south. What We Know So Far The 2024 MMWR report on dengue in the United States is the most comprehensive recent picture of the national burden. Of the 3,798 cases reported that year, 97.2 percent were travel-associated, with most acquired in the Caribbean, Central America, or Mexico. But 2.8 percent, approximately 106 cases, were locally acquired, a number that, while small in absolute terms, was significantly higher than in most prior years. The seasonal pattern is consistent and important: dengue cases peak between July and September, accounting for 41.6 percent of annual cases, according to the same MMWR. That means the current period, mid-summer 2026, is the highest-risk window of the year. Cases in 2026 have already passed 500 as of the brief period so far this year, continuing the upward trend that marked 2024. Florida reported 1,044 local and travel-associated dengue cases in 2024, more than any other continental state. California followed with 719 cases, driven largely by travel-associated infections in the Los Angeles metro area, though the documented local transmission chain in Los Angeles County has raised the profile of the state as an emerging risk area. Where the Risk Is Highest Florida remains the highest-risk state for locally acquired dengue in the continental United States. Miami-Dade County's subtropical climate sustains Aedes aegypti populations year-round, and the county accounts for the large majority of Florida's locally transmitted cases. Hillsborough, Pasco, Manatee, Monroe, Orange, Palm Beach, Broward, Sarasota, and Polk counties in Florida all reported locally acquired cases in 2024. Southern Texas and California's major metro areas present the next tier of risk. The more notable development is the northward range extension of Aedes aegypti and its close relative Aedes albopictus, commonly called the tiger mosquito. Published research from the University at Albany , released in September 2024, attributed dengue risk expansion in California, Arizona, and the Carolinas to the documented range extension of both species. A 2026 mosquito surveillance report projects continued expansion into previously unaffected northern states, with localized dengue transmission risk expected to grow in new geographies. In practical terms, residents of Charlotte, Atlanta, Phoenix, Los Angeles, and San Diego now live within the potential range of mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue. That does not mean dengue cases will inevitably occur in those cities, but the biological conditions are now present in a way they were not a generation ago. What Doctors and Experts Say The University of Florida's Emerging Pathogens Institute has noted that while no part of the continental United States is officially classified as endemic for dengue, Florida's health department continues to report locally acquired cases each year, and the risk is no longer limited to its southernmost counties. Researchers at the institute have linked the resurgence of Aedes aegypti in Florida, after a period of near-displacement by Aedes albopictus in the 1990s, to the conditions that have enabled more frequent local transmission since 2009. The CDC's public health guidance for jurisdictions facing dengue transmission risk emphasizes vector control as the primary intervention when Aedes mosquito populations are high, temperatures and precipitation support mosquito activity, and travel-associated case counts are elevated. All three conditions now apply in multiple U.S. metropolitan areas during the summer months. Puerto Rico remains the most severely affected U.S. territory, having reported 6,291 dengue cases in 2024, with more than 52 percent of those requiring hospitalization and 13 deaths. A public health emergency remains in effect there. What the Evidence Shows and What It Does Not The evidence that dengue risk is expanding in the continental United States is supported by multiple lines of data: CDC ArboNET surveillance showing rising case counts, peer-reviewed entomological research documenting vector range expansion, a confirmed local transmission chain in Los Angeles, and sustained activity in Florida. What remains uncertain is how quickly and how broadly that risk will translate into large-scale local outbreaks outside of southern Florida. The 2024 case spike was partly driven by historically high global dengue activity, which increases the probability that returning travelers will seed the virus into areas with competent mosquito populations. Whether 2026 continues that trend at the global level will affect how many importation events occur in U.S. cities this summer. The United States does not have a dengue vaccine currently recommended for general continental use. Dengvaxia , approved only for individuals aged 9 to 16 with prior confirmed dengue infection in U.S. territories including Puerto Rico, is being discontinued, with remaining stock expiring in 2026. No other dengue vaccine has received U.S. FDA approval or CDC recommendation for continental travelers or residents. Who Faces the Greatest Risk People at highest risk include residents of southern Florida, especially Miami-Dade County, and individuals who travel to Caribbean nations, Mexico, and Central America, where dengue activity remains common during summer and fall. Travelers to Puerto Rico face an ongoing elevated risk given the active outbreak status there. Anyone who has already been infected with dengue once, regardless of which serotype, faces a more serious medical risk from a subsequent infection with a different serotype. Older adults, pregnant individuals, and people with underlying health conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease are most likely to experience complications from either primary or secondary infection. Residents of cities in the Carolinas, Southern California, Arizona, and the Gulf Coast region should be aware that Aedes mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue are now present in their communities, even if locally acquired transmission remains uncommon. Symptoms and Warning Signs to Watch For Dengue symptoms typically appear four to 10 days after a mosquito bite from an infected Aedes mosquito. The classic presentation is a sudden high fever accompanied by severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, and a skin rash. The joint and muscle pain can be so severe that dengue is sometimes called breakbone fever. Most people recover within one to two weeks. Severe dengue, more likely in people experiencing a second infection, can cause bleeding under the skin, gum or nose bleeds, blood in urine or stool, persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, fatigue, and restlessness. Severe dengue is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalization. Anyone with these symptoms who has recently been in a dengue-risk area should seek emergency care immediately. What You Can Do Now Use EPA-registered mosquito repellents containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus, or para-menthane-diol on exposed skin whenever outdoors, particularly during peak mosquito hours from dawn to dusk. Wear long sleeves and pants in areas where Aedes mosquitoes are active. Remove standing water from flowerpots, buckets, bird baths, gutters, and any container that can hold water for more than a week, as Aedes mosquitoes breed in very small amounts of still water. Travelers planning visits to dengue-risk areas should consult the CDC's destination-specific dengue guidance before departure and report any fever or flu-like illness that develops within two weeks of returning home to a health care provider, with disclosure of travel history. Anyone experiencing a high fever with severe headache and joint pain within two weeks of returning from a dengue-risk area should seek medical evaluation promptly, as early diagnosis and supportive care improve outcomes. Cost and Access: What Patients Should Know There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Management is supportive, meaning rest, fluids, and pain relief with acetaminophen rather than aspirin or ibuprofen, which can worsen bleeding risk. Severe dengue requiring hospitalization is covered under most major health insurance plans. Uninsured patients who need hospital care for severe dengue should contact their county health department about emergency Medicaid enrollment or charity care programs. Dengue testing through a blood panel is available through most major diagnostic laboratories and hospital systems in areas where the disease is recognized. Clinicians in regions without prior dengue experience may need to specifically request arboviral testing panels. What Happens Next The CDC continues to update ArboNET dengue case data throughout the summer. Health departments in Florida, Texas, California, and other at-risk states are maintaining vector surveillance and issuing localized alerts as conditions warrant. Researchers tracking the Aedes aegypti range expansion are expected to publish updated findings before the end of the 2026 season. MedicalDaily will continue to track dengue activity in the United States through the fall. The Bottom Line Dengue is no longer a disease that only travelers returning from the tropics need to worry about. The record 2024 U.S. case count, the documented local transmission in Los Angeles, the sustained risk in Miami-Dade, and the confirmed northward expansion of the Aedes mosquito mean that more Americans than ever are living in areas where local dengue transmission is biologically possible during summer months. Strong mosquito repellent use, standing water elimination, and prompt medical evaluation for fever after potential exposure are the most effective protective steps available right now.
